content: Lesson 51 kept both halves in the past:
if + had done, would have done. But a
past cause can still shape the PRESENT.
PAST condition, PRESENT result:
if + had done ... would + plain verb.
"If I had taken the job, I would be in
Spain now."
"If she had spoken up at the time, her
conscience would be clear now."
Now the mirror. A PRESENT condition can
explain a PAST result:
if + past simple ... would have done.
"If I were more careful, I would not
have said it."
"If he spoke French, they would have
sent him."
Each half is marked for its OWN time.
Ask two questions: what is untrue now,
and what did not happen then?
Many languages set one mood across the
whole sentence; English times each half
on its own.
The past tense does not always mean past
TIME. After these three it means unreal
or urgent — and no if is in sight.
it's time + past:
"It's time he admitted he was injured."
= he has not admitted it, and he should.
would rather + past, about someone else:
"I'd rather he stopped playing now."
had better + PLAIN verb — no past here:
"He'd better rest for a week."
= a warning, not a preference.
Careful with the negative. It is
"You'd better not tell her,"
never "You hadn't better tell her."
wish and if only take the same unreal
past: "I wish I knew." "If only he had
listened."
Many languages keep a subjunctive for
this. English has no separate form left,
so it borrows the past tense instead.
Formal English can drop 'if' and invert
the subject and the helper instead.
"Had I known, I would have waited."
= If I had known ...
"Were it not for the rain, we would go."
= If it were not for the rain ...
"Should you need help, ring this number."
Only had, were and should do this.
Other ways to carry a condition:
unless = if ... not.
"Unless it rains, we walk."
provided that / as long as = only if.
"You may go, provided that you write."
otherwise = if that does not happen.
"Write it down; otherwise you forget."
It was a relief to hear it — but had he
called an hour earlier, nobody would
have worried at all.
Many languages keep one conjunction and
change the verb mood; English changes
the WORD ORDER and drops the if.
